subject: jukebox
reasoning:
I'm figuring out that building a jukebox prop with the SDK still requires a root joint internally, since the part resolver and weight calculations need at least one joint to work against, even though props themselves don't need articulation.

I want to model this as an iconic Wurlitzer 1015 "Bubbler" jukebox from 1946: roughly 1.6m tall, 0.8m wide, 0.65m deep, with a dark plinth base, a chrome-grilled speaker section, a record-mechanism window in the middle, and the signature arched dome top with glowing bubble tubes. I'm working out the vertical sections and proportions carefully since I won't get to visually verify the result.

For the front silhouette with its rounded arch, I'll extrude a 2D outline in the x-y plane along the z-axis, generating the arc points programmatically since the shape mixes straight edges and curves. I'm settling on final dimensions around 0.82m wide, 0.62m deep, 1.45m tall to keep the proportions true to the original design while planning the full top-to-bottom layout of base, grille, window, and dome.

I'll apply a walnut grain paint along the y-axis for the body's wood texture, then move on to shaping the arch window opening on the front face.

Since extrudes can't actually have holes cut into them, I'll fake the window effect by layering a chrome arch bezel in front of a dark inset panel — building up depth through stacked front-facing layers rather than true recesses. For more realism, I'll instead construct the cabinet from distinct parts: left and right side panels, base, and back.

Actually a simpler layered-plate approach fits a stylized model better: extrude the arch silhouette for the cabinet body with beveled edges, then stack front details on top — a speaker grille panel with chrome bars and gold trim, positioned on the lower front face.

Next I'm planning the mid-band with a chrome trim strip holding colorful selector buttons and a coin slot plate, then the arch window above it containing a stylized record carousel visible behind a chrome bezel.

I'm picturing records standing on edge, arranged radially around a vertical axis so from the front you'd see edges on the sides with one record face-on, like the Rock-Ola carousel design.

Working out the geometry so discs don't overlap near the axis — offsetting each disc's position radially and orienting its plane to contain the radial direction and the vertical axis, with normal tangential to the ring, so they spread out like a carousel instead of intersecting.

This reads like a pinwheel effect from the carousel, which is good enough and true to how jukebox carousels look. But the cabinet is a solid extrude, so I need to restructure it in layers to create a real recessed window opening where the mechanical interior can sit, rather than just a dark panel on a solid front.

I'm planning the hollow arch frame: a thick surround made of left and right stiles plus a curved arch band swept along a semicircle path with a box cross-section, combined with a back wall panel and floor for the window cavity. Since transparency isn't available through the shared material system, I'll need to build a separate glass mesh with its own standard material to get that see-through effect.

Actually, since every part should go through the builder rather than raw meshes, I'll skip the glass entirely and leave the window open -- it still reads well and keeps the interior visible. Now I'm working out the window geometry: straight sides from y=0.80 to 1.12, width 0.58, with an arched top radius 0.29, giving an inner apex around 1.41, and adjusting the outer shoulder radius to about 0.41 centered near y=1.05 to get a total height near 1.5.

I'm restructuring the cabinet's front silhouette: half-width 0.41, bottom at y=0.07, straight sides up to y=1.05, then a semicircular arch to an apex near 1.46, plus a small crown ornament reaching ~1.55 -- slightly taller than the real 1.43m reference but fine for stylization. The window opening sits inset with 0.12 margins on the sides and top, centered with its own radius giving an apex around 1.34.

Rather than a single solid extrusion, I'm composing the cabinet from a lower wood block (box roughly x ±0.41, y 0.07 to 0.80, z ±0.31), built as a rounded-rectangle extrusion with a slight bevel for a softer, more characterful edge instead of a plain box.
